issues.item: Hypervigilance towards people: vigilant for dangerous people
issues.explanation: These items suggest an interpersonal/physical danger trauma pattern (monitoring dangerous people, avoiding exposed spaces due to vulnerability), which is hard to reconcile with the stated trauma type of unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one unless additional assault/combat-type trauma is present.

issues.item: Avoid Open Spaces: Open or exposed spaces where I feel vulnerable
issues.explanation: For trauma involving the unexpected death of a loved one, avoiding open spaces due to feeling physically vulnerable suggests a different threat context (e.g., assault, combat, public attack) and is not clinically well integrated with the other selected items, which are grief-related. Within the Maladaptive Strategies node, 'Avoid Positive Feelings' and 'Avoid Grief Reminders' are coherent with bereavement-related PTSD, but 'Avoid Open Spaces' pulls toward a conflicting trauma/symptom pattern that is hard to explain from the provided formulation and item set.

vignette: Arthur Vance kept his hands moving on the wedging table long after the clay went cold, as if slowing down would let the past catch up. Five years ago, the phone had rung at 3:14 a.m. while he was sleeping in the guest room. His father had been out buying morning papers when his heart simply stopped. There was no hospital watch, no quiet passing, just a paramedic’s flat voice telling Arthur he needed to come down to the county morgue before there was time to prepare himself for the sight of a man who had always been solid. Arthur had arrived to a room that smelled of antiseptic and cold tile, to a body bag zipped partway up, to the sudden, irreversible finality of a life that ended without a single warning. He had come to believe that safety was an illusion, that any moment could strip him of what he held most dear. In the days that followed, the potter’s studio became both sanctuary and mine. Arthur started clearing his father’s old trimming tools from the shelf above the wheel. He began sweeping the workshop at dawn, long before his wife, Clara, woke, avoiding the quiet hours when the house felt too still. He could not bear the smell of roasted coffee left on the counter, the way the afternoon light hit the front porch exactly as it had on the day the police had knocked. Anything that brushed against the memory of his father became a threshold he refused to cross, so he moved through his days like a man navigating a room he had been forced to empty. When he worked the wheel, his hands remembered what his mind fought to suppress. The rhythmic pull of the clay felt steady until a particularly refined bowl caught the studio’s north light and Arthur felt a sudden, unbidden lift in his chest. He caught himself smiling at a customer’s compliment two days later, but the warmth vanished before it reached his eyes. He had come to believe that feeling good was unsafe, that letting himself relax meant he was betraying the suddenness of his loss. He would abruptly shift his weight, dampen his hands in the slip bucket, or abruptly mention the humidity of the kiln room to his apprentice, pushing the positive feeling away before it could take root. The avoidance of the future took a different shape. When the regional craft fair board sent their summer lineup, Arthur left the email unread. He stopped quoting prices for custom commissions, claiming he was working through a dry period. He had grown certain that making promises about next month, let alone next year, was like building on sand. He answered Clara’s questions about their anniversary dinner with vague shrugs, redirecting her toward household maintenance, because the word future had become a closed door. He told himself it was easier to stay in the present, where nothing could be taken away without warning. Over time, the studio felt smaller. Orders accumulated on his desk but never made it to the firing schedule. Clara began sleeping in the downstairs guest room, noting how Arthur flinched when she reached for his hand, how he treated every shared laugh like a temporary arrangement. He kept telling himself that keeping his circle narrow kept him safe. What finally brought Arthur to the clinic was the silence in his own workshop. He had spent the past Tuesday staring at a lump of stoneware that he could no longer justify throwing, realizing that his hands were working only to keep the stillness at bay. He sat in the intake chair now, terrified that if he let himself hope for a different kind of life, he would be caught off guard again. He did not want to lose his father to memory, but he did not know how to carry him without letting the weight crack his hands. He had come here because the quiet was no longer protective; it was just hollow. He hoped, however faintly, that someone might help him figure out how to live without bracing for the next phone call.
